At the end of the day, practically all games short of bug-ridden wrecks can be beaten with sufficient time, patience, and practice. Some however are so unfairly hard that you simply have to stop playing them or risk throwing your rig out of the open window from your third-story apartment.

One of the (very few) games that did this to me was Earth 2150: Lost Souls. The second expansion pack to the good but sadly not very widely known RTS Earth 2150: Escape from the Blue Planet, Lost Souls was clearly targeted at veterans of the series, but imho overdid it quite a bit with the difficulty.

In virtually all missions, the enemy bases are heavily fortified and full of mines that can instakill most of your tanks. Removing the mines with specialized vehicles is a no-go as they are fragile and will be shot up almost instantly, so artillery it is. Naturally you need not bother actually attacking the base until the AI has run out of resources, as the constant trickle of tanks the enemy churns out is enough to grind down an army of any size.

Still, once the enemy (and you) have run out of resources, you could raze the enemy base with concentrated artillery bombardment. Theoretically, that is. In practice, there are three issues making this annoyingly difficult:

  1. Ammo. As one of few RTS games, Earth 2150 features an ammo system in which units with conventional weapons (including two of the three artillery weapons) can run out of ammo. Airborn transports that load up ammo from a building in your base and then supply your vehicles in the field are needed to prevent your tanks from turning into sitting ducks. Unfortunately, most of the maps of the campaign have enemy anti-air guns all over the place, and as the ammo transports will always make a beeline to their targets, dozens of them can be shot down in a single mission. Compared to this, the Harvesters from Command and Conquer were tactical geniuses. Meanwhile, AI units never have to reload at all.

  2. Enemy spawns. As mentioned above, attacking the enemy base usually is only viable when both you and the enemy have run out of resources, making unit conservation on your part critical. The AI on the other hand gets entire tank battalions roughly every five to ten minutes. At best, these are a nuisance which temporarily prevent you from careful sniping the enemy base to pieces. At worst, you have 15 enemy bombers spawning inside your base.

  3. Hilariously bad unit pathfinding. As mentioned above, the enemy base usually is heavily fortified, and anything short of heavy tanks will be nigh-instagibbed by all the defensive turrets, making the use of artillery necessary. Sadly, the guys who drive said artillery vehicles often are not very bright. If, for instance a tree is blocking their line of fire, they will more than often drive straight up to the enemy building to shoot it at point blanc (or rather, try to do so and explode four seconds later).

Long story short, I eventually snapped after one particularly difficult and lengthy mission in which I already had destroyed most of the enemy base only to see an entire horde of artillery tanks materialize out of thin air, drive straight through my defenses, and then destroy the one key building I had to protect.

What games made you snap? (And by god, you better not mention Dark Souls).

One thing that Valve does really well is maps that point out where you go, what you do, and how to do it without making it obvious. They don't tell you, they have subtle hints in the maps. The building you need to go to? It stands out from the rest. The door you need to go through? The path you need to take? It stands out, but it isn't covered with signs/people telling you where to go. They let you figure it out.

For example, the generator stalled in Ep 1. The power went out. The player follows the "electrical cable" and figures it out themselves. You need to break through that barrier? Good thing someone left this cart loaded with heavy stuff at the top of this hill! The player looks around and says "I can use that!" The combine soldiers who wave when you are not looking at them, and they are the only one attacking you? Catches your eye, and you now see them. Small subtle hints to make the path/goal/target obvious to the player without directly giving them the answer. Nobody says "Use X to do Y", there is no sign that says "HEY, LOOK THIS IS THE ANSWER".

That is what Portal Stories: Mel is missing in the maps. The subtle map hints in how it is designed that say "Hey, this is how you solve the puzzle!" without actually telling the player "This is how you solve the puzzle!"

Dark Souls didn't make me quit out of frustration. It frustrated the hell out of me and then bored me until I forgot about it with two bosses left in the vanilla version + all DLC bosses.

I was enjoying it, despite the ruthless game mechanics, until I got to the Ornstein and Smough fight. For those not familiar, it's a fight that pits you against two bosses that has one of the steepest learning curves I've ever seen in a boss fight. There is a pattern and a strategy and there are people who can win the fight regularly in speed runs and NG++ playthroughs, but the first time you go up against them it's just a wall of ultra cheap tactics and infuriating mechanics.

Some examples: * Ornstein can cross a massive cathedral floor in a couple of seconds, making extending to regroup non-viable

  • That alone wouldn't be too big of a deal but he can also attack and kill you through large stone pillers (arm and weapon clip right through) which eliminates cover as a reliable strategy as well.

  • After you kill one, the other gets a super buff. They were nasty enough to begin with. The super buff is pretty harsh.

  • If you get clipped by their super maneuver, or you don't know all of their emotes and attacks, you're dead. And if you were a sliver of health from killing the second one when you die, they'll both be back waiting for you when you return for the next attempt.

  • You have to run a short distance from where you respawn after death to the boss arena, and there are some large enemies just outside the gate. After you pass through the gate into the boss arena, the monsters outside can and often do still clobber you with their halberds which can stagger you in addition to the damage they day. It's just a little extra cheap on top of a cheap sundae.

At some point I'll go back and finish the DLC and remaining vanilla bosses, but after Ornstein and Smough, my enthusiasm to play just became less and less as everything seemed contrived and cheap instead of genuinely challenging.
